questions.q: Name three supporting characters in "laofn;k" and give one defining trait for each based on the text.
questions.a: Correct answer: (1) Badi Gosyani — talkative, manipulative, acts as the host who summons the storyteller; (2) Badi Chhutki — extremely old, frail, tells stories in a hypnotic voice, embodies the fading oral tradition; (3) Chhoti Maa — practical, protective of her son, skeptical of the storyteller's motives. A wrong answer that lists only "old women" or "villagers" without distinguishing traits shows the student cannot differentiate characterisation from mere presence.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how Badi Chhutki's storytelling differs from Gajakshaphu's and why that difference matters.
questions.a: Correct answer: Badi Chhutki tells stories from lived memory, in a slow, hypnotic rhythm that puts listeners into a trance, while Gajakshaphu performs professionally for survival. The difference matters because it shows storytelling as a communal ritual (hers) versus a commodified skill (his). A wrong answer that says "both tell stories" misses the contrast between organic tradition and professional performance — a central tension in the story.

questions.q: Find two moments in the text where Chhoti Maa's dialogue reveals her distrust of Gajakshaphu. Quote or paraphrase each and explain what her suspicion tells us about the village's attitude toward outsiders.
questions.a: Correct answer: (1) When she asks "क्या लेन-देन बाकी है?" after Gajakshaphu claims he has settled accounts — shows she monitors transactions closely. (2) When she warns "तुम्हारी माँ... तुमको छोड़कर चली जायेगी" — reveals she sees through his emotional manipulation. Both moments illustrate the village's sharp, transactional wariness toward itinerant performers. A wrong answer that picks random lines without linking to distrust shows inability to connect dialogue to character motive.

questions.q: Compare the narrative function of Badi Gosyani and the driver (who takes Gajakshaphu to the village). How does each move the plot forward in a different way?
questions.a: Correct answer: Badi Gosyani initiates the central conflict by inviting Gajakshaphu and setting the storytelling event in motion; she is the catalyst. The driver merely provides transportation and background information about the village's changed condition; he is an expository device. A wrong answer that treats both as "minor characters who help the hero" fails to distinguish catalytic agency from functional utility.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "Badi Chhutki is the most important supporting character because she represents the authentic voice of the village." Defend or refute with textual evidence.
questions.a: Correct evaluation: The claim is partially true but incomplete. Badi Chhutki does embody authentic oral tradition (her stories put the whole village in a trance), but Chhoti Maa represents the village's pragmatic survival instinct, and Badi Gosyani represents its gossipy social fabric. Together they form a triad of village voices. A wrong answer that simply agrees or disagrees without acknowledging the ensemble nature of the supporting cast shows reductive thinking.

questions.q: Write a 150-word scene from Badi Chhutki's perspective describing Gajakshaphu's arrival, using her voice (slow, sensory, rooted in memory). Include at least two details from the text reimagined through her eyes.
questions.a: A strong answer will use first-person, present-tense narration with sensory details (smell of dust, sound of cart wheels, feel of cot strings), reflect her frailty and authority, and incorporate textual facts: e.g., Gajakshaphu arriving in a cart, Badi Gosyani's summons, the village's changed layout. A weak answer will write in third person, use modern vocabulary, or omit her distinctive slow rhythm — showing failure to internalize character voice.
